opus-5.5.text:
I think for me it came down to whether the questions they cared about were the same questions I kept coming back to on my own. During my PhD I spent a lot of time on robot learning, and the thing that bothered me most was that so much of the field felt like one-off demos: you'd get a policy working on a specific task in a specific lab, and then it wouldn't transfer anywhere. So the real question for me was: is anyone seriously trying to build something general, a foundation model for physical behavior, rather than another clever trick for one task?

When I talked to people at Pi, what stood out was that they weren't just saying "general-purpose robots" as a slogan. They had very concrete, sometimes opinionated views on what would actually matter: data at scale and diversity, how to combine pretraining from vision-language models with robot data, how to think about action representations. And they were willing to argue about it. Some of the conversations felt less like interviews and more like research discussions where we didn't fully agree, and I took that as a good sign. If everyone just nods along, you don't learn much.

The other thing I paid attention to was how they treated uncertainty. In robotics a lot of things simply don't work the first ten times, and I wanted to be somewhere that is honest about that, that runs real experiments on real hardware and lets the results change their minds. I got the sense that the team valued taste: knowing which problems are worth pushing on, and which are distractions.

And honestly, part of it was the people. A small group where you could tell everyone was senior enough to have strong intuitions but still hands-on. I wanted to be in a place where I'd be challenged every day, and where the bar was "does this move us toward generality" rather than "does this make a nice paper." That combination is what convinced me it was the right fit.

r001.rationale: The response says the team was honest about uncertainty, ran real experiments, and let results change their minds, presenting this as a positive sign of fit.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it wasn't a very systematic process. I think the biggest thing was just talking to the people. When I interviewed, the conversations didn't feel like interviews, they felt like arguments about robotics. People would push back on things I said, I'd push back on them, and nobody seemed to care about defending a position just because it was theirs. That told me a lot.

The second thing was how they talked about failure. A lot of labs, when you ask what's not working, you get a polished answer. At Pi, when I asked, people would just pull up videos of the robot doing something dumb and say, "yeah, we don't really understand this yet." That kind of honesty about where the frontier actually is mattered to me, because it meant the problems I'd be working on were real problems, not marketing problems.

And then there was the question of taste. I wanted to know whether their bets matched my intuitions about what's important. At the time I believed pretty strongly that the bottleneck in robotics was data and generalization, not clever control. When I talked to Sergey and Chelsea and the others, it was clear they'd arrived at a similar conclusion, but from a different angle and with more evidence than I had. That's the ideal situation, right? You agree on the direction but you'd each add something the other doesn't have.

I'll also say, part of it was a gut thing. I remember leaving the office and feeling like I'd learned something in a single afternoon. That doesn't happen often. If a place makes you feel smarter after a few hours, you should probably take that seriously.

r001.rationale: The candidate says people challenged one another’s ideas without defending a position merely because it was theirs, which communicates a truth-seeking attitude and its role in judging intellectual fit.

astra-6.text: For me, the key was whether we could have a productive research conversation. During recruiting, I wanted to understand what people thought the hard problems were, why they were taking a particular approach, and what evidence would make them change their minds. I was also paying attention to whether I could ask basic questions and disagree openly. You don’t need to agree on everything to have a good intellectual fit, but you do need to feel that thinking together makes your ideas better. That was the feeling I was looking for with Pi.

r001.rationale: The response describes looking for people who would explain what evidence could change their minds and engage openly with questions and disagreement, signaling a truth-seeking attitude as a sign of fit.

sol-6.1.text: For me, it was less about whether everyone agreed with my ideas and more about how we could think through a problem together. During recruiting, I tried to get a sense of what people thought the important problems were, why they thought those problems mattered, and how willing they were to question their assumptions. Those conversations were my way of judging whether Pi would be a place where I could contribute and keep learning.
